speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, farmers in Canada listening to the debates in this House on Bill C-l 10, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, are perplexed and angry with the priorities which the Government holds. Providing the Export Development Corporation with a credit of $62 billion is a bewildering contradiction for the farmer who seeks Farm Credit Corporation assistance, only to be told that the Corporation has no funds.
The EDC legislation proposed by the Government permits the extension of credit at below market rates of interest in order to promote trade, and this suggests to Canadian farmers that the same type of consideration should be made available to them.
If the Government of Algeria is deserving of a $100 million loan at 7 per cent, 10 per cent less than the cost to Canadian taxpayers of borrowing that money, and the purpose of that loan is to construct a monument to Marxism, Canadian farmers rightly ask, "Why is money not available to us through the Farm Credit Corporation for infinitely more legitimate purposes and, when it is available, why are we not given concessionary interest rates such as are available to offshore customers?"
Surely if the Government of Canada considers that Canadian exports require the type of financial commitment which Bill C-l 10 provides, it is not too much to suggest that agriculture, the largest job creator in the nation, should be deserving of equal treatment.

Mr. Speaker, many western Canadian grain producers are facing critical financial problems. Some farmers in my constituency of Brandon-Souris have told me that if they do not receive payments soon from
the Western Grain Stabilization Program, it could be the last straw. They could go bankrupt.
One would think that the Stabilization Program, to which each farmer contributed up to $1,200 this year, would have the flexibility to make payments when the payments are needed most. And in fact the program is in a very good position to do so. There is more than $800 million in the fund now. By April, 1984, there will be close to $1 billion in the fund. That is the most money the fund has ever contained in its history. However, the final decision has not yet been made on whether there will be a payment for crops seeded in 1982, and here it is September, 1983. Western grain farmers need the money now.
I urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to consider basing the calculation on a three-year rather than a five-year average so that the calculation reflects up to date conditions. As well, there is no justification for a 12-month delay, or even longer, between the time the crops are taken off and the time the payments are made. As it now stands, the program, despite all its money, does little to stabilize the western grain production industry.
We need a revised Grain Stabilization Program and, even more, we need a new Government, a Government that cares about the Canadian farmer.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REMISSION OF SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all well aware of the way in which the present income tax system discriminates against residents of northern Canada, but another tax problem which acts to the detriment of the few northern manufacturers has not received such widespread publicity. If an article is manufactured in the south, say at a cost of $100, and then transported to the North at an additional cost of $100, the final cost will be $200, plus federal sales tax levied only on the first $100, for a total of $209. If, however, the same article was manufactured in the North, the cost including transport of materials and the additional costs of northern operation, would likely be $200. Federal sales tax would then be levied on the full $200 to bring the total cost to $218. Therefore it is evident that the federal sales tax works to the disadvantage of the northern manufacturer compared with his southern competitor.
The solution which ought to be implemented is for the granting of partial sales tax remission for certain northern firms, in the same way that customs duties are frequently remitted for many southern firms when they can demonstrate undue hardships.

No Member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty, nor of any of the Royal Family, nor of His Excellency or the person administering the Government of Canada; nor use offensive words against either House, or against any Member thereof.
Also in support of my suggestion that the Chair might wish to pay closer attention to the contents of statements made under Standing Order 21, I refer to page 21873 of Hansard for Monday, January 17, 1983, when Madam Speaker was in the Chair discussing the application of the new experimental rules. She said:
There are two areas in particular where the discretion of the Chair will be a significant element in the successful operation of the provisional rules.

September 23, 1983

The second area is the procedure, provided for in provisional Standing Order 21, which will enable Hon. Members other than Ministers to make statements of not more than one and a half minutes on matters of concern.

All questions raised must be on matters of concern, but they do not necessarily have to be matters of urgent and pressing necessity. I think that in the previous application of Standing Order 43, the Chair had to consider the content of the motion, but in this case, and in this particular form. The House resumed from Thursday, September 22, consideration of Bill C-110, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs; and Motions Nos. 6 and 8 (Mr. Blenkarn).

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to have the opportunity today to contribute to the debate on the amendments which have been

September 23, 1983
Export Development Act
proposed by my colleague for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn). All of us in this House recognize the necessity of trade for Canada and the important role that the Export Development Corporation plays. We in this Party have no desire to undermine the EDC or prevent it from making its contribution to Canada's economic wellbeing.
It is difficult to see how several of the provisions in the Bill will substantially improve the ability of EDC to function. Instead, in our opinion the measures in this Bill, which we hope to amend, serve only to thwart Parliament's role.
As Members will recall, the Auditor General stated in his 1982 report that "Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of Government activities". He also said that it is Parliament's "fundamental responsibility for overseeing receipts and expenditures of public funds". Most of us in this House take that responsibility very seriously, and this Government is making it increasingly difficult and frustrating for those of us who want to fulfil our responsibilities to the people who sent us here.
Bill C-110 is just another in a series of attempts by this Government to pursue its interventionist policies and philosophies at the expense of Canadians. Members will recall that the Canada Development Investment Corporation, the most dangerous Crown corporation yet, was formed without a single word of debate in the House of Commons. The Government now wants to have access to additional billions of dollars to do with as it sees fit, without having to inform Parliament of its intentions or to ask for our approval.
The measures in this Bill will further subvert Parliament's accountability. The Government is continuing to follow the examples it set with CDIC, Canadair, de Havilland and Consolidated Computer. By introducing measures such as this, the Government is attempting further to thwart the ability of Members of Parliament to control the purse strings. We are being asked to give the Members of the Cabinet and a board of directors, which could conceivably consist of 15 public servants, virtually a free hand to deal with billions of dollars. We have plenty of examples from the past and from other Crown corporations which would make the most charitable person wary of the monetary management abilities of this bunch.
Ironically, the Liberal Government no longer considers Parliament to be the central institution in the parliamentary system of democracy. Rather, it sees it as something to be avoided, a block in the path of its way to having its interventionist policies permeate everything. It looks upon Parliament not as the central institution of our democracy, but as an obstacle, a pain-in-the-neck, something which must be tolerated and, if at all possible, avoided.
A perfect example is the lack of willingness on the part of the Minister to entrench in legislation the need for a board of directors on the EDC to come from the private sector. The problems caused by having Government representatives on the board of directors have been well documented.
In his testimony before the Public Accounts Committee in the Canadair fiasco, former Liberal Cabinet Minister Jean-
Pierre Goyer, the Vice-Chairman of Canadair, outlined some of these problems. For example, he pointed out that the public servant is subordinate to the Minister and must deal directly with him. His public servant status does not allow him the leverage he may need in dealing with the Minister in matters concerning the Crown corporation. In the case of EDC, this involves at least six public servants, and usually more. If the board members were more independent of the Cabinet, perhaps their opinion as to high-risk or abnormal transactions would be better respected by the Governor in Council.
It is difficult to understand why the Government is so anxious to increase the amount of outstanding funds available for authorization by the Governor in Council from $3.5 billion to $10 billion for insurance deals. It has as yet used less than half of the current $3.5 billion authorization. Does the Government have any plans in the near future for such a large sum of money? If so, I as one Member of Parliament would certainly be interested in hearing about those plans, as I am sure would everyone else on this side of the House.
Likewise, a jump of $7.5 billion in the funds available to Cabinet for authorizing loans and loan guarantees is quite exorbitant. It is very difficult to imagine the existence of that great an increase in demand for guarantees.
However, Mr. Speaker, all Members of this House are reasonable people. If there is such a demand for loans and guarantees and if providing for them would benefit Canadian exports and our economic position, I am certain we would willingly give our approval. Unfortunately, Bill C-110 would not allow any opportunity for discussion or debate of such decisions in Parliament. Parliament would have no say in the distribution of a possible $20 billion.
The lack of accountability is totally unacceptable, not only to those of us in the Official Opposition but to many others, including the current and past Auditors General, members of the Public Accounts Committee, the Lambert Commission, the Economic Council of Canada and more. It is time for our friends opposite to wake up and recognize that the policies they are following are not welcomed by Canadians.
In 1979 when this Party was in Government, we introduced a solid piece of legislation designed to return control and accountability of Crown corporations to Parliament. That legislation was commended by many, including the Auditor General. Indeed, in the latest Auditor General's report which was issued in December of last year, the Auditor General compared Bill C-27 with the Government's proposals and he found the Government's proposals grossly deficient in comparison.
The Government has chosen to ignore the initiative that was taken by the Conservative Government when it tried to bring some element of control and accountability to Crown corporations. Instead, over the course of the past three years we have seen a steady attempt by the Liberal Government to downgrade the role of Parliament, to avoid parliamentary scrutiny,
September 23, 1983

and to avoid parliamentary control over the purse strings which belong to the people of Canada.
If the Government will come before us in the House to ask for confidence and to ask for access to more taxpayers' dollars, surely it has the responsibility to us and to the people of Canada to demonstrate that it merits that confidence. It must demonstrate that in its behaviour to date it has deserved to gain access to that sort of money. To date, nothing could be further from the truth. The Government's track record in the economy and its performance with the myriad of Crown corporations it has created over the years has been dismal. The prospects for serious scandals in the future and for great losses of public funds continue to grow.
Let me ask this of you, Mr. Speaker, since I know this is a matter that is of particular concern to you as you are a vigilant observer of the way the Government operates and you are deeply concerned by the need to protect the public purse strings. If you had $100 to invest, Mr. Speaker, which one of these Ministers would you trust to invest that $100 on your behalf? Would it be the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan)? I think not. You are too prudent to accept a proposal like that, Mr. Speaker. Would it be the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais)? Certainly not. Is there anyone who sits on these Treasury benches whom you feel qualified to invest your $100, Mr. Speaker, anyone who would not simply lose your money? I see, Mr. Speaker, from your expression that you would have nothing to do with them, and certainly Hon. Members on this side of the House would agree.
If the Government wants more authority and wants to intervene in the economy further, if it wants to have greater access not only to your money, Mr. Speaker, but to the money of all Canadians, then the time has come for it to demonstrate that it merits that confidence on our part. Its actions and the performance of its Ministers to date indicates that there is no cause for such confidence. I think Canadians have every right to expect that Hon. Members on this side of the House and indeed Hon. Members on all sides would support the motions which were moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), so that we may do everything we can to rein the Government in and to restore to the purse some element of parliamentary control.

Mr. Speaker, 1 certainly intend to listen to your advice by ignoring the Chair entirely during my remarks.
I hope that the hon. gentlemen opposite are in a mood to listen today so that I do not have to get excited and lose my train of thought while I address them.
We are, of course, discussing this Bill within the context of today's economic conditions. The economic conditions of the country today have occurred as a result of the last 20 years of rule by the hon. gentlemen opposite. They might be interested in hearing about some of the statistics that apply to what has been happening in the field of exports during that period of time. They might be interested in knowing that between 1969 and 1979 we suffered a 33 per cent decline in Canada's over-all share of world exports. That 33 per cent decline indicates that we declined in importance in the field of export trade with respect to the rest of the world. Our performance was the worst among industrialized countries during that period of time.
In 1968 our share of world trade was 5.2 per cent. In 1981 it was 3.6 per cent, even though during that period of time the present Minister responsible for external affairs who was then the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce went to the private sector in an attempt to boost our exports. Those were the results of the Minister's efforts. Thank God he is not in that area any longer, or perhaps he is back in that area at the moment.
Statistics are wanton forms of lies.

As the Hon. Minister points out, statistics are closely associated with the field of prevarication. I take that as read because we hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) using statistics every day to prove the opposite of what the facts are. As an example of that, Mr. Speaker, this week we saw that the Minister of Finance had the gall and the audacity to make a speech on September 15 in which he said that Canada was leading the world in the rate and pace of its recovery. Every other independent economic forecast during that week was to the opposite effect. Canada is not leading the world in anything but loss of potential, loss of opportunity and loss of the ability to accept the challenges that are offered. Those are the areas in which we are leading the world, not the area of recovery.
As I pointed out to the Hon. Minister in Question Period, if he were to be correct in his statement, my response would be: "Stop the world, I want to get off." If Canada is leading the industrialized world in its recovery, stop the world and let us get off. It is not worth being here any longer.
That is the context in which we can look at statistics. We saw a report by the OECD today. The Government did not want to deal with it. That report points out that the unemployment prospects in Canada are much worse than the Government had forecast in its budget of last April. It forecast a rate of over 12 per cent this year.

September 23, 1983
Export Development Act
During today's Question Period, the question of fisheries came up. The fishery is one of the main exporting industries of the country. A tremendous amount of fish is exported from Newfoundland, for example, to the United States, yet the Government, in the last two or three months, has embarked upon a plan with the Bank of Nova Scotia designed to put the offshore fishing industry of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia into receivership. It has interfered with the exports of fishery products from Newfoundland and Labrador to the United States of America. Today the Government is backing the Bank of Nova Scotia in court in an attempt to have its receivership over the Fishery Products Limited confirmed. During the last several weeks, while this attempt to put that firm into receivership was under way, the export from Fishery Products Limited to the United States has been interfered with to the tune of in excess of $1 million per week. The Government does not appear to be too concerned about the export of fish products or the economy generally.
The motions that are before the House have more to do with control and accountability. In that context I want to bring to the House's attention a point that was made by Don McGilliv-ray in one of his columns in Southam News this week about the share of the Gross National Product now being spent by the federal Government. He said that Governments together, federal, provincial and municipal Governments, are now spending-at least, the statistics show this-for the three months that ended in June, 47.4 per cent of the Gross National Product. Governments between them are taking almost half the GNP in this country.
An every day you are asking for more.

The Minister says that every day we are asking for more. What we are asking for is less, spent in a more efficient manner.
On January 12, 1980, during the election campaign when he set out his economic platform, the Prime Minister said that he would not increase federal spending as a proportion of the GNP and that he was going to contain Government spending within the growth of the GNP. That promise was made when the federal Government was taking about 15.8 per cent of the GNP under the eight-month Clark administration. Today we discover that the federal Government is taking over 20 per cent of the GNP in taxes and through revenue-gathering measures. The Government is spending this money.
Even during World War II the Government only achieved the level of taking 22 per cent of the GNP, at a time when all levels of Government took only 30 per cent of the GNP. During World War II when taxation in this country was savage, all Governments between them took 30 per cent of the Gross National Product of Canada from the citizens and spent it themselves. Today, when there is no war, over 47 per cent of the GNP is being taken by these same Governments.
I make that point because that is the fundamental error in the Bill. The Government is giving too much authority to the
bureaucrats; the Government is giving too much authority to the Crown corporations; the Government is giving too much authority to civil servants generally. There is no accountability by the Export Development Corporation to Parliament nor to the people of Canada. It comes before a parliamentary committee perhaps once a year to be asked questions. Parliamentary committees are parliamentary units in our system of Government; they have no independent powers. Members have ten minutes to ask questions and to be buffaloed around by the persons to whom the questions are addressed, so there is no accountability. The EDC is one of those Crown corporations that is not accountable to the House. If the legislation now before the House is passed, it will be even less accountable for more money than it was before the legislation was passed. That is why we are opposing the Bill.
I would think that a Government should be glad to give Members of the House more power. This is the attitude I would have if I were a Minister, and will have if I am a Minister when the change of Government comes about consequent upon the calling of the next election. We know the next election will not likely be called until March, 1985. We know the nervousness in the Government ranks. We saw them act like a group of burbling school girls in Question Period today. They are so nervous when a question is asked that they have to laugh nervously and applaud any kind of bunkum they hear from the Ministers who are supposed to answer. There has to be an election in 16 months and then there will be a change of Government.
Any wise Government will enlist the help of the House of Commons in the job of controlling the bureaucracy. Ministers' offices do not control the bureauracy. The minister of state for foreign affairs, I think he is called now-
External Relations.

The Deputy Prime Minister is the Minister in charge of external relations. The Minister here is in charge of foreign affairs. I do not know what the difference is-how foreign affairs differ from external relations. In any event, when he was Minister of Transport he had no control over the bureaucracy. He did not know what was happening in his department.
The Minister who is now Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) and who was in charge of the Post Office was so ignorant this summer that he did not invite me to his ceremonies in honour of producing the Sir Humphrey Gilbert stamp in Newfoundland which I had spent a year and a half writing and asking him to approve. When he had the ceremonies in St. John's at the Arts and Culture Centre this summer, he was too ignorant to invite either of the sitting Members of Parliament. He invited the Hon. Member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons), since elevated to the heights of Cabinet. Ten days later he descended from the heights to the depths. He knows now about the sharp teeth of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) and what the bureaucracy is like. That is by the by, Mr. Speaker. The Minister showed a pattern of ignorance. I was right in St. John's when the ceremonies took

place, with free drinks and liquor splashed out. Ele produced the Sir Humphrey Gilbert stamp that 1 had harassed him for 18 months but he never even asked me to the ceremony. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I would not have gone even if he had asked me. I do not associate with bad company in my own district.
1 will come back to the point I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker. Ministers do not control the civil service. They do not really know what is happening in these boards and commissions and Crown corporations. Why would they not welcome Members of the House having some real powers to make independent inquiries about what is happening as long as it was understood that they were not going to topple if they were not personally involved in situations that were uncovered? One would think that Ministers would welcome the assistance of Members of the House and its committees in an attempt to make the bureaucracy more responsive and more responsible. They do not control them, but they do not want anyone else to control them either. That is illustrated in the Bill, Mr. Speaker.
1 notice from my extensive file that the Liberal Member for Manicouagan, Mr. Maltais-I am not supposed to use his name in the House but 1 want to give him adequate publicity-made a pitch to the Catholic bishops. He said he wants them to take leadership in economic affairs. Export Development Act

Mr. Speaker, in entering the debate on Motions Nos. 6 and 8 to amend Bill C-110, an Act to amend the Export Development Act, I do so not out of any concern that the trading life of our nation is not important, but rather out of a deep concern that is represented across Canada and across southwestern Ontario regarding the finances of the nation and the control of our resources. The Kitchener-Waterloo area depends upon trade. It also has a tradition of frugality and responsibility in the investment of the resources which are available to the people of that area.
I enter this debate, Mr. Speaker, to underline the concern of the Official Opposition, and a concern which is reflected in my area, that trading opportunities for Canadian businesses be enhanced. The issue here, of course, as my colleagues have indicated-and we have now had well over 100 representations on this theme-is parliamentary accountability. The Bill which is before us would permit $62 billion in non-accountable funds for the Export Development Corporation. The EDC, of course, is not required to table an operating budget. It is not required to table a capital budget or information on the size of its payroll, which is something which normal investors would expect.
We are aware, of course, Mr. Speaker, that the EDC has to date borrowing authority of $10 billion. However, as of December 31, 1982 it has used approximately $4.5 billion. The argument is not that we are holding up any export financing whatever in our opposition to this Bill. Rather, we wish to underline the importance of the role that the Canadian taxpayer plays in the procedures followed by the Government of Canada.
There are a large number of reasons, of course, for opposing this action which have been mentioned by my colleagues. It is inefficient, for one, with ten employees per loan and one and one half employees per insurance account.
A second factor is that the board of directors is composed of too many public servants. The exporting in this country is done mainly by private sector companies. The EDC should, therefore, have a strong private sector representation in order to balance the input from the bureaucracy.
A third factor, which is in front of all who are concerned about this issue, is the difficulty which was outlined in a recent article in The Globe and Mail, the difficulty in dealing with the agency. Export deals, the article reports, have been lost because of the procrastination of the EDC and its excessive requirements for financial guarantees.
If one needed a fourth reason it would be that when the EDC does arrange loans, they are more often than not to the same companies. Nearly half the 1982 business went to Bombardier and Spar Aerospace. The question must be raised by concerned Canadians, are these subsidies becoming a form of permanent assistance to these companies?
Motions Nos. 6 and 8 which were proposed by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) will limit the amount of money which the Cabinet can commit to bad deals.

September 23, 1983
Export Development Act
With respect to Motion No. 6, under the current EDC Act sometimes the board of directors is not prepared to approve a proposed insurance deal because it would, "if entered into or issued, impose upon the corporation a liability for a term, or in an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake in relation to any one contract, person, commodity, service or country, or in relation to any particular contract, person or commodity". In other words, it is a bad deal. Under these circumstances, Cabinet can nonetheless approve the transaction. The money comes from the Consolidated Revenue Fund without need for parliamentary consent.
As it stands, Cabinet can commit up to $3.5 billion. This Bill would increase that amount to $10 billion. To date, only $460 million has been used, even under the current Act. The Cabinet, therefore, still has some $3 billion left. Now the Government wants $6.5 billion more.
With respect to Motion No. 8, the same provisions are in place for loans and loan guarantees as are in place for insurance deals. Cabinet can take from the Consolidated Revenue Fund up to $2.5 billion. It wants to increase this now to $10 billion. Again, the corporation has used only about $750 million of its $2.5 billion, and thus has about $1.75 billion left. This is again to be used for suspicious deals which the EDC would not touch with a ten-foot pole.
The two amendments to the Act which we are debating, and which we are seeking to annul, would bring the total amount of money available for these deals to $20 billion from its current already too high level of $6 billion.
As I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, there is concern about the instruments of investment, and of encouragement of the free enterprise system across our country. I hear it from farmers. I hear it from small business people. 1 hear it from taxpayers. The Auditor General's Annual Report seven years ago underlined that in the majority of Crown corporations management control has been weak and ineffective. Four years ago the Lambert Commission underlined this. Last year the Auditor General underlined this. Therefore, the public as a whole is not unaware of this situation.
The Kitchener Chamber of Commerce last year undertook a review of the Auditor General's Report and in its review it writes:
-we have continued concern, as does the Auditor General, with the significant waste and inefficiency in the federal government bureaucracy. In particular, we are much concerned with the very apparent use of Crown corporations for political purposes to avoid public scrutiny of government policy and ineptitude.
Motions Nos. 6 and 8 seek to redress this wrong. If the deals which the EDC refuses and Cabinet approves are not inept, or made for political purposes, why did the EDC turn them down? The Kitchener Chamber of Commerce believes it is necessary for Crown corporations to be constantly monitored and scrutinized. Given the horror stories about the abuses and excesses of these corporations, this is not too much to ask. The suggestion by the President of the CNR this past week that there ought not to be an audit of that company only fuels this
concern. This Bill, if unamended, will do nothing to allay these fears; hence the motions.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Kitchener Chamber of Commerce suggests that the purpose and relevance of Crown corporations should be clearly explained to the people of Canada and constantly monitored so that they continue to exist only if their purpose can be properly justified to the taxpayers. I suggest this Bill manifestly does not do this. All in all, the government of Canada can decide to take on unsavoury export transactions by Order in Council, appropriate money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to do so, and shove the matter through as a statutory advance without any reference to Parliament or its committees whatsoever-no debate, no vote, no questions. This is not good enough for this Party. It is not good enough for the people of Canada who, after all, have their earnings invested through tax dollars in this way.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps 1 should begin by welcoming Members across the way back from their extended lunch hour. It is very important that all Members of the House understand the importance of trade to Canada both today and throughout recent Canadian history. We on this side of the House want it to be clearly understood that we recognize the importance of trade since Canada is and has been an exporting nation. It is imperative that we continue in that tradition.
As we know, this country began essentially as a primary producing colony. It was a colony of France, at which time its livelihood was gained by the export of furs to France. It later became a colony of Great Britain and the nature of its economy changed somewhat. It depended upon the export of furs, then timber, potash and subsequently wheat and other agricultural products.
Today, of course, the economy of Canada is much more diversified than it was in the past but it remains, nevertheless, very dependent upon the export trade and upon those nations and neighbours with whom we have developed extensive com-
September 23, 1983

mercial relationships. We on this side of the House recognize the importance of agencies such as the Export Development Corporation. But we are very disturbed by the changes in legislation which are currently before the House in Bill C-l 10 because we fear that these changes will make the Export Development Corporation much less accountable to the House than has been the case in the past and much less accountable to the House than either we on this side or the people of Canada would wish.
The point we wish to reiterate is that the Export Development Corporation in a sense is performing a very useful function in strengthening the trading sector and particularly permitting the export of processed goods to countries which have not traditionally been our customers. However, it is extremely important that this corporation operate in a way which is fully accountable to the principles of Government as they have traditionally been developed in Canada. It is extremely important that that corporation remains directly accountable to the Parliament of the land.
It has come to our attention, and hence we hope to the attention of Canadians, that there is provision within the Bill currently before the House which, unless it is amended as we propose it, should be amended, will permit the Export Development Corporation to operate in a way which is essentially non-accountable to Parliament. Furthermore, the Cabinet, by order of executive council, will be able to operate in a way which is even independent of the will of the Export Development Corporation and thus be non-accountable to Parliament.
The amount of money which the Export Development Corporation and Cabinet can spend without being directly accountable to us is mind boggling. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the total is some $62 billion. In fact, the sum of $62 billion is so horrendous that it almost requires repetition in order for the point to be effectively made. The $62 billion which the Export Development Corporation and Cabinet could expend over a period of time without answering to Parliament is such a huge sum that one must compare it to other sums in order to make it meaningful. Of course, the amount of $62 billion even makes the deficit which the Government across the way has accumulated this past year look small. The Export Development Corporation will have the authority under this Act to insure up to ten times the amount of its authorized capital.
This Bill proposes to increase that authorized capital from $1 billion to $2 billion. It will then be able to insure a total of $20 billion. It will then be able to insure a total of $20 billion, again without direct authorization by or accountability in this Parliament. In addition, the Export Development Corporation will have the authority to lend up to ten times the amount of its authorized capital. That is another $20 billion. The Cabinet will have authority by Order in Council to lend up to $2.5 billion without the concurrence of the EDC.
By the way, under this proposal the EDC is essentially managed by those who work on behalf of the Government. This Bill would increase that $2.5 billion to $10 billion. That is another $10 billion which could be spent without direct accountability. The list goes on. Another $10 billion can be
Export Development Act
spent by Order in Council, without direct accountability, in the field of insurance.
Finally, the Bill proposes to increase equity in the corporation from $1 billion to $2 billion. That is a total of $62 billion, all of which is obtained without honouring the principle of direct accountability.
There is ample evidence throughout Canada that there is a tremendous, growing apprehension on the part of Canadians about the decline in responsible Government as they understand it. As I walked about the lawns at noon hour I recognized that there are statues which heed the contribution in the past of those who worked and fought for responsible government. The essence of that responsible government is the relationship between the Cabinet and the Parliament of this land. The essence of responsible government is that the Cabinet shall be held accountable to Parliament for its actions and hence held directly accountable to the will of the people of this land.
Unfortunately, the powers which are contained within this legislation that would permit this Government to expend the amount of money we have been talking about by Order in Council means that we will have a diminishing of that responsible Government. In fact, it seems to me that we are moving in the direction of the American model where there is, in fact, a separation between the legislative arm of government and the executive arm of government. We in Canada who operate under the British parliamentary tradition have never accepted that model of government and we feel that it is extremely reprehensible that steps are being taken in that direction.
In order to support my contention that Canadians are distressed by what is happening, I would like to quote briefly from a working paper prepared by a committee of the Canada West Foundation. This is a very distinguished body whose activities are well known in western Canada. In this paper we find:
The Canadian parliament at the moment has a number of obvious and important defects which can be summarized as follows: a growing inability to monitor the financial operations of government; a growing inability to control the regulatory activities of government; virtually no control over the policy initiatives of a majority government and a perceived distance from the real needs of the electorate.
Those who wrote this brief were very well informed of the intentions of those across the way, and their comments are exceedingly well taken. This brief goes on:
The parliamentary system we inherited at confederation has evolved in a manner that has strengthened the control of the executive branch.
That is the Cabinet. The paragraph continues:
There is no other truly democratic state in the world where the legislative branch is so supine before the executive. A Canadian Prime Minister or Premier in his own jurisdiction is the absolute ruler. The result is a four year elected dictatorship, should the incumbent choose it to be so, and this is one of the reasons for interest in parliamentary reform.
The words I have quoted are the words of those who wrote this working paper on behalf of the Canada West Foundation. It seems to me that the point which they made is extremely

September 23, 1983
Export Development Act
germane at this time. Legislation which is before the House will enhance the power of the executive arm of government. It will diminish the authority of those of us who are part of the legislative arm of government. It will set back the concept of responsible government as we know it, and it will set back the system of responsible government as known by those who worked so hard for it in the nineteenth century.
It is imperative, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments currently before this House proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party be sustained.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-110 and in particular on Motions Nos. 6 and 8 moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), and seconded by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp).
I rise with a great feeling of responsibility toward the proposals put forward by my colleagues to counter the Government's proposals to increase to $10 billion the limits on contingent liabilities and on loan guarantees for the EDC. I say a great feeling of responsibility because the issue here is accountability, and the responsibility of this Chamber. The Government is trying to make the issue in this Bill and in the various amendments into an issue of trade. The issue is accountability and the responsibility of this Chamber.
For more than ten years I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. For the last three and a half years until this week I was chairman of that body. I think it is fair to remind the House that that Committee, like all others, has a majority of members of the Government in its membership.
I have served on that Committee under five different chairmen, including Mr. Hales, a former Member of this House; the present Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse); the present Hon. Member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence); the present Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington); and the present Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston). In all of those years the Public Accounts Committee was striving, along with many other people, whom I will mention in a minute, for accountability to Parliament and accountability to the taxpayers for all branches of government. Today we are dealing particularly with Crown corporations, in this case, the Export Development Corporation. I say we, along with many other agencies here, were working for the same ends. There were many studies initiated by the Government. The Auditor General himself has reported many, many times on the failure of the system to provide proper accountability to the legislators, to this House and to the taxpayers.
I think it is fair to note that many of the reports of the Public Accounts Committee have been concurred in by this House, but not necessarily acted upon by the Government. Many other reports of the Public Accounts Committee sit on the Order Paper right now awaiting only a motion for concurrence. I would not expect the Government to concur in them without some kind of a fight, but I think the Government
ought to remind itself that those reports came from a committee which was made up of a majority of Government members.
One might ask why accountability is so important to the House and to the taxpayer. It is simply because of the enormous amounts of money involved.
The total debt of the Government of Canada at the end of the 1982 fiscal year was $134 billion. That is gross debt. The net debt at the end of that fiscal period was $95 billion and projections for the next three or four fiscal years brings that net debt up to $232 billion. That is an increase in the total net debt of the Government over the next four years of about 2.5 times.
Some people say that having a lot of debt is not so bad. After all we have revenues and we can pay off that debt. But debt is not free of charge. It does not come without the attendant interest responsibility. Years ago it might have been fairly easy to pay the rates of interest which, say, 50 years ago were 3 per cent and 25 years ago about 6 per cent or 7 per cent. But in the past few years, Mr. Speaker, we have seen rates of interest exceeding 20 per cent, and the average for the past seven years or so was about 15 per cent. I do not have an actual figure, but it was in the range of 15 per cent.
The costs of that interest are reflected in the estimates of the Government. We can see in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1983 that the federal Government's interest costs were over $16 billion. That amount is just about equal to the total budget of the Government of Canada about 12 years ago in the 1972 fiscal year. Debt is not without its costs. We must emphasize at every possible opportunity what a huge amount of non-productive expenditures is being taken out of our budget every year by the cost of carrying our debt.
The effect of the Crown corporations on the total financial picture of the Government is another very important factor that is frequently overlooked. In the first place we have over 300 Crown corporations; nobody is exactly sure how many. At the last count Crown corporations employed some 263,000 people, which is about half the total number of people who work for the Government of Canada.
Crown corporations have not in general had unfaded reputations. A few come to mind. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited was allowed to get out of control. Now as a matter of government policy, it is borrowing $100 million every year in order to pay for the cost of production of heavy water that no one needs. It is being stored in a field in barrels in Atlantic Canada. Nobody knows why except that it is Government policy. It is an idiotic Government policy when we have enough heavy water on hand to last five years at the projected rate of sales of reactors.
After nearly two years the Government answered a question which I had on the Order Paper concerning the expenditures of Petro-Canada during the period from 1970 to 1980. I asked what shares or other ownership interest Petro-Canada had acquired in any other corporation. I received an answer to my question this week indicating that Petro-Canada acquired a
September 23, 1983

100 per cent equity in Atlantic Richfield Canada Ltd. at a cost of $342 million. It did not have this money so it had to borrow it. Interestingly enough, the book value of those $342 million worth of shares was less then half, or $126 million.
Then it acquired 100 per cent of the equity of Pacific Petroleums Ltd. at the cost of $1,496 billion, which was nearly three times the book value. Petro-Canada did not have that amount of money to spend so it borrowed almost $1.5 billion for that acquisition. Also it acquired 45 per cent of the common shares of Panarctic Oils for $80 million, and 15 per cent of Syncrude Canada Ltd. for $315 million during the same period of time.
My question was dated in 1981, and I did not request a longer period of time. If I had done so, I would have found out in answer to the question about other acquisitions, one of which was Merit Oil Ltd. of Vancouver. Petro-Canada acquired it in the name of Canadianization, which is quite a laugh because that corporation was already totally Canadian owned.
Other Crown corporations which have been and will be more and more in the news are Canadair and de Havilland. The Government should come clean with its policy intentions with respect to them. The previous Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was responsible for issuing loan guarantees for Canadair. He should admit that it was Government policy to follow a certain course of events, rather than let the new Minister from the other place come along and blame management for spending a lot of money leading up to the unprecedented write-off of $1.4 billion. It was clearly Government policy that that course was followed.
I see Mr. Speaker starting to rise, so I will finish with one sentence. The Government claims that EDC is impoverished at the same time as it is clear from the facts before us that there are hundreds of millions of dollars still unexpended in the money already available to EDC. These amendments should be supported by all Hon. Members.

Mr. Speaker, in joining the debate on the two amendments now before us, I feel it will be helpful if I emphasize that there are really two types of loan activities in which the Export Development Corporation can engage. There is what one might regard as the normal corporate lending activity, and then there is Order in Council or Government type lending activity. The amendments of my colleague touch upon the second type of lending activity. In short, it is the concept that where EDC feels, for reasons presumably known to it, that it does not wish to lend to whatever level is being requested, the Government can step in and give additional money through the clauses we are now considering and attempting to amend.
We must bear in mind that we are not talking about $100 million or $1 billion. We are talking about $10 billion of authorization. If we in our wisdom in this Parliament decided to pass the clauses the Government is asking us to okay, it would mean that these Order in Council or Government type loans of the EDC could go up to a ceiling of approximately
Export Development Act
$60 billion between insurance and lending activity without any further parliamentary authority. It is extremely important that Hon. Members of the House bear this in mind.
Most of us have probably been pressured by groups which are benefiting from this type of financing. It is lobbying; that is what it is. We are told that we must get on with passing this Bill because the EDC cow may run out of milk, that they are enjoying the milk and the cream very much and would like it to continue. My colleagues have made it abundantly clear that we do not want to see Canada just participating as we have been doing in world trade, just accepting a 3.6 per cent share of world trade, but getting back to the old 5 per cent fair share of world trade. There is no disagreement on that question. In seeking to secure more trade, we must analyse whether we are being prudent in the amount of authority and authorization we are giving to the EDC and, in the specific clauses we are now considering, to the Government.
Let me put it into perspective, if I may. When it comes to the question of whether we are crowding or somehow being unfair to EDC when it requests a $60 billion authorization, let us not forget that as of December 31, 1982 the total corporate and Government lending activities, the total assets of the EDC, were $6.5 billion. That is the total amount it expended as at the end of 1982. It is asking for authorization to make it ten-fold bigger compared with its total assets at the end of last year of roughly $6.5 billion.
What is even more revealing is who has been the benefactor. As we all know, the Export Development Corporation publishes a statistical review every year. In its 1982 review it listed its lending activities under the corporate side and under the Government side. If Hon. Members would take the opportunity to read who are the benefactors, perhaps for the first time, if they have been doubting Thomases, they would see why we are so concerned about what the Government is attempting to do. The fact is that the statistical review of EDC revealed that during 1982, between Government lending activity under the Act and corporate lending activity, Bombardier Inc. of Montreal secured authorizations which will involve future financing from EDC or the Government directly of $957 million. In truth, when we compare that with the total commitments of EDC during 1982, we find that Bombardier, one company alone, received almost 40 per cent of the benefit of its commitments for that year.
Let me put that into perspective. Who is Bombardier Inc.? I invite Hon. Members to take a look at the annual report of Bombardier Inc. There is a familiar name on the board of directors of that company which will perhaps bring it into focus.

Mr. Speaker, is it not rather amusing; 1 have not even mentioned the name yet. The Grits are so sensitive

that they fear that I might inadvertently mention the name of a Liberal. On this one point, the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) has guessed right. He is beginning to learn what his colleagues are up to.

I hope the Hon. Member for Mississauga North comes across the country with me because he would be of real assistance. He has reminded me that included in the Bombardier financing through the Export Development Corporation was a sale to the almost defunct New York Transit Authority. If we read the same statistical review, we find that the United States Metropolitan Transportation Authority of New York got two cracks at the Canadian public purse. Directly from EDC it received $294,912,000. The Government stepped in with another $626,688,000. Isn't that nice! Talk about a milk cow! It was so blatant in the United States that the U.S. Commerce Department instituted an action in that country, pointing out that in its opinion the Canadian Government had provided a subsidy amounting to $167,225 for each subway car proposed to be sold to the Transit Authority of New York.
Can you believe that this Government, which denies financing to help commuters get to work in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver, is willing to subsidize authorities in New York to help workers there get to and from work through a company which happens to have a very friendly director on this board.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to intervene with respect to Motions Nos. 6 and 8 put forward by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I had an opportunity to address the House in this matter when we were dealing with Motions Nos. 3 and 5. At that time I raised two important issues about this Bill generally which many Members have been able to deal with as they indicate clearly why we on this side have stood against the Bill.
First, we were able to point out in those motions with respect to the corporation that for years the Conservative Party has indicated to the Government over and over again the importance of international trade to the future of this country and the need to have the financial facilities necessary for that growth if we are to become world competitive and world class in our economic endeavours. It has taken a long time for the Government to understand that.
When the Government brought forward this Bill, it was gross with respect to the amounts of money involved in it, far beyond the needs of the corporation vis-a-vis our prospects for international trade. A number of people indicated with respect to this corporation that there were clear, honest and sincere complaints from prospective customers about the ability to be able to export, that the corporation has been unable to accomplish those things which many people want to have happen. We raised those issues in order that the Government, particularly the Ministers involved, would pay attention.
Not only was there the question of the corporation, but a second issue was raised at that time, that of Crown corporations. At that time I pointed out that since 1962, 21 years ago, we have gone from 28 Crown corporations to over 300. We now have assets of $74 billion and liabilities of $63 billion. What has happened in those 21 years has been an enormous growth in the size, power and lack of accountability of Crown corporations. That is what scares many people.
Crown corporations are not controllable. They are certainly not being controlled by this Government. There has been a long and honourable tradition of Crown corporations in this country, which has had to grow in a large geographical space with a small number of people. These people had to depend upon public enterprise. The emphasis from the first public enterprise corporations has always been on public scrutiny and public accountability. That is why I complained at that time and I have not heard anyone say nay to it. In the 15 years that this Government has been in power, the honourable Canadian tradition of public accountability of corporations has developed into a situation where billions and billions of dollars of taxpayers' money lie unaccounted for.
Those are the two issues raised in Motions Nos. 3 and 5 and which affect Motions Nos. 6 and 8. Motions Nos. 6 and 8 bring into focus the most important aspect of this Bill. It is true that the question of the usefulness of the corporation to its customers is important. It is true that the question of Crown corporations is an important issue. By far the most important is not those two issues, but the question of the relationship of those corporations to this Parliament. The crucial issue in this Bill is the responsibility and accountability to Parliament, to the people who elect us. It is not possible for the people who elect the Members who sit in this Chamber to hold them accountable for the functioning of those Crown corporations because this Government has taken away the ability of Parliament to hold those corporations accountable.

At the root of it all, the most important issue here, is parliamentary control and parliamentary responsibility. Anyone who understands the history of that issue knows that we in this country enjoy our freedoms and privileges. You, Mr. Speaker, enjoy your privileges on our behalf, and all Members of this House on behalf of their constituents, because of the link between Parliament's control of the public purse and the rights of a free people to be able to control their governments.
There has been warning after warning, year after year, which the Government has ignored. There were warnings from the Lambert Commission, the reports of the Auditors General, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, the Economic Council of Canada. Over the past 15 years that this Government has been in office, those agencies have warned us year after year that the Government's ability to control public expenditures was beyond control.
My point is that this is not merely an issue of public accounting and it is not merely a question of corporations, however important that may be, as my friend, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) has indicated. It becomes finally a question of how to limit the power of Government.
In 400 years of development, the only way we have been able to do that is to limit the power of Government to raise and spend money. Throughout the whole history of the development of our Parliament and indeed the history beyond these shores, all the historical struggles which established the rights of this Parliament and the rights of the people of the country were related to accountability to the public in the raising and spending of taxes. There can be no taxation without representation. That is pointed out by the rules of this House and was established by the historic fight between the Crown and the Parliament.
It is easy to let this control slip away. One thing that people take for granted, unless they lose it, is freedom, individual liberty. That is easily and best defined as freedom from the power of Government to control. Our ability to control the power of Government lies with our ability to control its expenditure of funds. That is why this issue is not only a question of financial corporations. Ultimately it is a question of the power of the House to control on behalf of the people of the country the power of the Government. That is why we have spoken against this Bill and will continue to speak against this Bill, Mr. Speaker.
It is absolutely essential that the Government, after 15 years, finally understand that we in the Conservative Party will not allow it to continue to drive the public's ability to control expenditures out of the Chamber. When that happens, we embark upon a downhill slide which will include the loss of our ability to control the other actions of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, once again I am pleased to speak to the very important principle that is embodied in Bill C-110. We in the House forget, and in fact

the Government has forgotten, that governments do not have money. It is the taxpayers who have the money.
As the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) has said, the issue at stake in this Bill began with the fundamental birth of a Parliament which exists to control the public purse and to protect the taxpayer. That is because it is the taxpayer and not the Government who has the money. Parliament oversees the spending, the delivery and the effectiveness of that money for the social good of the country.
The federal Government, because of its deficit, takes over 70 per cent of the term savings generated in the country. That means that there is not much left for others to do the work of becoming efficient, creating productivity, creating jobs and searching for world markets. As you know, Sir, the amendments we are now dealing with are Motions Nos. 6 and 8. With these amendments we are trying to prevent the Government from increasing its spending authority and power from around $6 billion to over $20 billion.
The Export Development Corporation is a Crown corporation which has really become a dinosaur. I was very pleased to be present to hear my colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), point out the nature of the favouritism and the narrow channel of delivery that is involved in the spending of these massive sums of money under the control of the Export Development Corporation. As was pointed out, almost one-half of Export Development Corporation business for 1982, $2.46 billion, went to Bombardier and Spar Aerospace. The other half went to de Havilland on 12 contracts, Massey-Ferguson on four contracts, Trico on three contracts and Northern Tel on three contracts. In 1982 EDC served only 62 exporters.
Let me now turn to the issue that really troubles me. The officers who sit at the desks of the Export Development Corporation are not interested in the rest of us. It seems that the creation, management and delivery of the Export Development Corporation is for the benefit of Crown corporations, corporations controlled by Crown corporations and the people within central Canada.
In my riding alone there are eight or nine shipyards. Those shipyards have put consortiums together that allow them to build some of the beautiful ships that are being built and have been built for the North Sea oil development, for the Arctic and for the fishing industry. The Caribbean and South America are markets for these ships. Two or three of these shipyards will get together in a consortium and put together a package for the designing and building of a small fleet of ships which will cost in the order of $1 million to $1.5 million each and offer them for sale to a South American or Caribbean country. It is almost impossible for that application to make its way past the initial desks of the Export Development Corporation.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, I can remember having to intervene on behalf of those consortiums in order to get a $3 million, $6 million or $7 million contract approved or insured through the Export Development Corporation so that those important payrolls in my riding can be met. I think we must wake up and realize that one of the problems with the mindset

Export Development Act
and attitude of the Export Development Corporation is that everything must be enlarged for an economy of scale, and that attitude trickles down from the Government.
That is the dilemma that is faced by the country. If we were to return to small, good quality working communities and pay attention to sectors of industry that could put together packages of good technology, we could earn our way back into the world markets. However, that leadership is not coming from the Government.
The Government is concentrating power, sucking from the people of Canada all of their disposable wealth, and it is delivering it in the form of a subgovernment created through these Crown corporations. There is no doubt that you have heard in this debate already, Mr. Speaker, about the growth of Crown corporations since 1962. In 1962, some 20 Crown corporations existed and were put in place to serve the public need with some kind of social sense. Today the growth and proliferation of Crown corporations creates jobs and advancement for people in the civil service. They now exist to further control the purse strings of Parliament and to further remove those purse strings from Parliament.
One of the most dangerous things that is happening today is that non-budgetary powers are being transferred to Crown corporations through the types of legal trickery that are involved in this Bill. If we began to take an inventory of the non-budgetary dollars or dollars that are non-discretionary which have been transferred to equity positions in Crown corporations since 1968, we would be truly startled. Maybe I should try to formulate a question for the Order Paper that would ask how much money, detailed by year, in non-budgetary terms has been transferred from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to the world of subgovernment, which includes the Export Development Corporation.
It has been said many times, and I am going to touch upon it again-and I know that you, Mr. Speaker, have been involved in this-that all we are asking for in this House is for the Government to accept report No. 7 along with the other reports from the Special Standing Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures. That report asks for four basic committees to deal with accountability. One of those would cover Crown corporations and quasi government bodies. We are entitled to an inventory and we are entitled to research expertise so that we can represent the people of this country properly. We must be able to formulate the right questions and demand answers in order to expose and disclose what is going on as a result of the Crown corporation malaise. This is vital because Bills like Bill C-110 remove more and more power from Parliament over the process of supply. We are delivering [DOT]more and more spending powers and statutory and non-budgetary processes over to Cabinet and Order in Council decree.
We have to review the behavioral problems in this culture that are taking advantage of and abusing every sense of trust, through to the Auditor General's Report. We could list chapter and verse, list after list and page after page of problems.
Crown corporations are even guilty of double invoicing in order to transfer profits offshore. Things like this cause great anguish and would end up in the courts if they were done in the private sector.
Crown corporations are given special preserves in terms of law. Being agencies of Her Majesty's gives them special status and protects their behavior and gives them special status when borrowing from the private sector.
These are questions that we want answered, Mr. Speaker. This is why, for the second time in this debate, I stand to protest and appeal to the Government to pull back on this kind of legislation. Give us a breathing spell and bring in some accountability.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to follow the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). He was talking about the basic ingredient of what Parliament is all about. We have the democratic institutions of today because of the people of the world who believed that if moneys were to be extracted from them, they should have something to say about the way they were spent.
We are making an argument that is as old as democracy itself-that there has to be accountability by the Government for the money it extracts from the taxpayers of Canada and then spends.
As we have gone through debate on Bill C-UO, speaker after speaker has given us many examples of the tremendous proliferation of Crown corporations and their belief that they are sacred and unassailable and that it is impossible to examine their activities.
Only this week I was shocked to see that the Chairman of the CNR, Jack Horner-a former Member of the House and one who stood on many occasions to talk about accountability and the requirement to have Members on the Treasury benches account to us for the money spent, supposedly on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada-was reported as saying that he did not believe the Auditor General should audit the books of the CNR. That is exactly what we are saying he should do.
Because somebody already does it.
Not on behalf of Parliament.
Yes.
The working papers are not available to Parliament and the report of the expenditures of the CNR is not part of the Auditor General's Report.
That is for sure, but the private auditors are responsible to Parliament.

It is a private audit for the private information of private people. Whether it is the Export Development Corporation, the CNR or one of the 298 Crown corporations that today employ more people than the Public Service of

Canada, we say that there should be greater accountability to the people of Canada. We are quite willing to be as generous with assistance to the business community and to help them make international trade agreements as any group in the House. What we want to know is where the money they get from taxpayers is being spent, if it is being spent properly and recovered properly. We do not know that. Parliament does not know that. Nobody knows that but the board of directors, and they are basically public servants.
That is another thing that is wrong with the EDC, Mr. Speaker. The people who put most of the roadblocks in the way of the business community in relation to trade deals are the same people who sit on the board, supposedly to assist the business community and negotiate deals that will provide employment.
The Government cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. They cannot have a man sitting in a Department one day, reading regulations and imposing them on the business community, and hours later have the same man sitting on the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation. As a director of the corporation he is supposed to aid and assist the industry, but he has just made the rules and regulations, and will impose them, that will make it almost impossible for the industry to make a deal. Can he say, "Let's look favourably at the type of assistance this company is applying for because I know the problem it is facing, as I manufactured most of them"? Why get into this situation when former corporate individuals, now retired or now not involved or having any vested interest, could be on the board? They would know how difficult it is to operate in the business community of the world and would appreciate the competition a company faces.
These companies claim they need this type of assistance, they need this type of interest rate, they need this type of loan, in order to achieve the end objective, which is a contract. However, what is happening now is that there are too many soft loans being made, and that is what we are concerned about. Too many loans are made which later end up as liabilities to Parliament and to the taxpayers of Canada, and we cannot find out about them. There is no one we can call to give us the reasons why such a loan was made, and that is not right or proper. Every board of directors in this country has a group of shareholders to whom it must explain every expenditure which is carried out. The Government is now asking us to give it between $50 billion and $60 billion so it can pass out loans-to whom? We do not know for sure. For what term? We do not know for sure. Under what conditions? We do not know for sure. If it is a success, that is fine. Let the board of directors come and tell us how useful it has been. However, if it is a failure, let the board of directors appear before us, as the protectors of the tax dollars, which are in fact trust dollars, and explain why such a loan was made which later turns out to be a liability for the taxpayers and the people of Canada.

I do not really understand how a government can stand by, on such a basic issue of parliamentary democracy, and ignore the requests of a legitimate opposition who is demanding that further protection be included in a piece of legislation for the taxpayers of this country, who are the people who put up the money in the first place. It is nothing short of a shocking scandal that this Government will sit by, to a major degree, and not even involve itself in the debate, and by its silence totally ignore the positive, progressive and realistic amendments which will improve the legislation before us and give greater protection to the taxpayers of this nation. More than that, these amendments will strengthen this institution. After all, it was the Boston Tea Party which led to the American Revolution. The Boston Tea Party was all about taxation without representation, and what we have in the piece of legislation which is before us now is taxation without representation.
The Government is taking money from the pockets of the taxpayers and it is unwilling to protect them by allowing the Parliament of Canada to examine the expenditures which are being made. As the Hon. Member for Capilano has pointed out, it is not because this Government has not been warned time and time again by the Auditor General of Canada, a non-partisan individual, that the way it is doing business does not give ultimate protection to the taxpayers of Canada. We, in the Opposition, have said quite clearly to the Government of Canada that this legislation fails in its present form because it does not provide accountability. We have moved amendments to bring about accountability and which would answer some of the concerns and criticisms of the Auditor General. Surely we can expect the Government to act, and react, and say, "Why not accept this amendment? It does not hurt us". As a matter of fact, it improves the piece of legislation. It also puts a new onus on the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation because when it does examine the loan applications which are made, it is going to know that eventually it will have to answer to the people of this country for the decisions it makes. That is what we seek. That is a legitimate requirement, a legitimate request, and I hope the Government will reconsider and amend the legislation, as we suggest, so that the taxpayers of Canada will have the protection which does not exist at the present time.

I do not think anyone in the House does not acknowledge the importance of international trade in all of our communities. I certainly am aware that the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), a colleague of mine on this side of the House, may be the greatest exponent of the need for international trade if we are to survive as a trading nation. Within my own constituency it is extraordinarily important that we have international trade. For example, one company by the name of Babcock & Wilcox, prior to the recession, used to have a payroll in excess of $60 million and employed over 1,800 people. They depend today almost exclusively on trade.
Fairness compels me to say that the EDC has been very good in its relationship with Babcock & Wilcox. I am the first person to acknowledge the fact. I have talked to the president of the company and I know that there has been a good

relationship and we have prospered. It is important particularly from my perspective because my own community has unemployment of close to 20 per cent-the alleged recovery in the economy has yet to occur there-and Babcock & Wilcox now employs less than 800 people.

I would like to see some Members on the other side at least acknowledge that there are substantial issues with respect to accountability and the choice of who the management ought to be in the interests of the nation as a whole. They cannot sustain the risk or do not think it wise to sustain the risk in a particular case.

I hear the Minister, whom I know and respect very much. He has had experience in this field. At the end of my comments I invite him to make a speech and talk about what I hope are his concerns about accountability and the issue of management with which he is intimately familiar.
Frankly, I have acknowledged that trade is one aspect of this Bill and an important one which is of concern to my constituency. I hope that by equal use of reasoning and frankness, he might stand up in his place as a senior and respected Member of the Government and talk about accountability and the prodigious sum of money that we are talking about, namely, $62 billion. I invite him to talk about the lack of control of the Parliament of Canada to deal with the taxpayers' money. If there is one thing that constituents are saying loud and clear from every constituency in this country, it is that they want their Members of Parliament to consider more seriously the expenditures. They want Members of Par-

liament to have some type of real control over the purse strings.
I say to the Minister, who wants to make a point-I know the Chair will give him every opportunity to do so as soon as I am finished-that I invite him to talk about these issues because they are significant.
Let me expand upon the circumstances where the board of directors of EDC does not think it is worth the risk for this country to make a deal with another country. This concerns the issue of management and who should be on the board of directors. I would feel much more confident, and I expect the Minister responsible for this Bill might feel more confident, according to some of his submissions, if the board of directors were at least controlled by competent people from the private sector. I would have a lot more confidence in a board of directors that had had experience in making decisions in the private sector. This is a circumstance where the board of directors may very well turn down a loan, whether it comes from the private sector or public sector, but the Government still says that it is in the public interest that it lend the money.
I would like to talk about the Bombardier bomb, as far as I am concerned. The Minister is here and I again invite him to make some remarks. We know that on a government to government basis, the Bombardier deal was worth $1 billion. We know that, in spite of the lip service that Americans pay to free trade and free enterprise, they have protectionism just like every other country. The "buy American" projects and advertisements that we see certainly give evidence of this. However, because of the serious economic plight of the City of New York and the fact that the deal was economically advantageous to that city to the tune of over $300 million, the firm of Bombardier and Budd were able to sustain this contract. There can be no doubt that jobs were the prime reason why the Government of Canada acted on behalf of these two particular companies.
However, 1 think we should closely examine the liabilities, how much work was going to be created and whether or not it was worth the candle. The Bombardier deal was to yield 20,000 to 25,000 man-years of work over the five-year life of the production. The United States would get 40 per cent, and the jobs that would be created would be based mostly in Vermont. Canada was to get 60 per cent. Three thousands jobs were going to be created in Canada over that period of time. The cost would be $325 million. To be conservative, assuming the cost of financing was going to be $300 million, there would be 15,000 man-years of work created at an average cost of $20,000 U.S. per job year. I believe the Government either neglects or fails to come to grips with these prodigious sums of money.
In conclusion, I wish to reiterate that the question is how one defines the issue. Is the issue to be defined with the primacy given to trade, or is the issue really a question of management or mismanagement and, most important the primacy of Parliament and the accountability of this Government to the people of Canada. That is why I stand to oppose
