Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to the amendments to this Bill. Briefly, the intent of the amendments is to simply limit in different ways the borrowing that the Government can undertake according to this Bill. I am fully in support of such amendments.
In short, this Bill appears to take up to $2 billion from our taxpayers upon which to borrow many billions more and use that money to subsidize interest rates for the foreign customers of Canadian exporters of manufactured goods. In other words, they will be helped to borrow money to buy our goods. In effect, our exporters and manufacturers get their price, the banks, which are mainly ours, get their price for the money, and the difference is carried by our taxpayers. Our taxpayers are subsidizing the banks since most working Canadians pay a higher tax rate than the banks effectively pay.
I think this is a very dubious deal for working people in Canada. Therefore, I believe it is a good idea to limit that borrowing. I am happy to support the amendments from the Conservative Party even if its reasons for the amendments might be different from mine.
There is another side to this problem. I believe a growing quantity of our sales are in the Third World countries, for example, the Philippines. I became interested in the Philippines through immigrants in my riding. I was astonished to find that one of the main exports of the Philippines is labour. About one milion people are "exported" from the Philippines as labourers who are compelled, as a condition of going abroad to work, to remit money home. That is a major source of currency for the Philippines. University graduates from the Philippines come here to work as house maids because of the extreme poverty there. I read about the Philippines in a very interesting book called the "Development Debacle". I have even had an opportunity to visit the Philippines very briefly this month. Part of the problem is that Philippines must buy our capital goods for their industries and for their infrastructures, such as their power supplies to industries. They must borrow. They are in hock to our banks, those in the United States principally. Canada tags along. Even though in the last ten years the real wages of Philippines have been cut by 50 per cent and the real price of rice produced by their farmers has been cut by 50 per cent and even, according to World Bank figures, people in the Philippines are eating less per capita than ten years ago, they still have great difficulty repaying these loans. According to the daily papers in Manila, they are dodging around the same kind of bankruptcy as we hear from time to time are occurring in Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and South Korea. There has been a growing number of strikes, bitter strikes in the Philippines. Strikes have occurred in the Bataan export processing zone. Now there are the riots in Manila that we have been reading about.
My point is that our borrowing system of asking the banks to subsidize sales by Canada to countries that cannot afford to pay for our goods does not really help those countries; it helps the banks. It does not help the working people or the farmers in the Philippines. It is very doubtful to me that this borrowing system is helping Canadians. Therefore, for that reason as well I am happy to support the sense of the amendments of the Tory Party.

Mr. Speaker, in this House last night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) rose to speak in defence of Bill C-110. As is the norm, he gave a very entertaining performance. It was so entertaining that the House called him back for two curtain calls in the form of being given unanimous consent twice to continue. I repeat, he gave a very entertaining performance in defence of Bill C-110, an Act to amend the Export Development Act. I think I am safe in saying that the farmers of Canada would be much more impressed if the Minister of Agriculture had used the opportunity to tell Canadians, and in particular Canadians who are engaged in agriculture, just what it is he proposes to do in the form of specific relief for some of the problems that agriculture faces. Perhaps, instead of bearing on the EDC, the Minister of Agriculture might have told us what he proposes to do to expedite stabilization payments, which are now running four or five months behind the norm. Okanagan farmers are struggling to keep ahead of the banks, and at the same time as the Minister talks about how great it is to be able to afford the Export Development Corporation's $62 billion in credits, farmers cannot get their stabilization payments. In the Okanagan the disastrous prices received for the 1982 apple crop have triggered a stabilization payment to Okanagan orchardists, but as yet they are still in the negotiating aspects preparatory to receiving that payment.
The Minister of Agriculture also, instead of concerning himself with the merits of Bill C-110 and what a great thing it is to provide $62 billion through this corporation, might have taken the opportunity to tell us why the Farm Credit Corporation has no funds, why the Farm Credit Corporation must put money out to farmers at a rate considerably in excess of what the EDC can offer to foreign customers of Canadian products. The Minister of Agriculture, who rose so quickly and so enthusiastically to defend the Export Development Corporation and to endorse that tremendous amount of money which that agency of Government would have available to it, could have brought great joy to Canadian farmers by indicating his reponse to their difficulty.
With The Canadian farm economy in a shambles and a spirit of despair and gloom hanging over the agricultural community, the agri-business industries, the Canadian farmers would like to have seen their Minister zero in on the things important to them, the important things which caused them to rally in Penticton on Labour Day and clog the highways with their tractors just to emphasize to Canadians, and the Minister in particular, that they are in a great deal of difficulty.
These orchardists are asking that action be taken right now before they are forced off their farms. They are asking for
September 23, 1983

tariff protection simply on the basis that you cannot let the tail end of another country's production set the price which Canadian farmers can ask for their product. As much as anything the farmers of Canada are asking for recognition, recognition of their importance to the nation and to the nation's economy and recognition that agriculture in Canada is in crisis.
Bill C-110 gives the recognition of the Government of Canada that export trade is important to Canada. It underlines that by making $62 billion available. That is the degree of recognition which Bill C-110 and the Government of Canada say is important. That is the degree of recognition which measures the amount of importance the Government gives to exports.
This recognition is given substance by the $2 billion capitalization which it permits and by the borrowing authority of the corporation of ten times that amount, that is, $20 billion, by giving authority to accept insurance liabilities to a further $20 billion, by allowing Cabinet to authorize $10 billion in dubious loans, and by allowing Cabinet to accept liabilities in the form of insurance contracts of an additional $10 billion, for a total liability for the taxpayers to assume of a maximum of $62 billion. That is an incredible amount when one considers that the total budget of the Canadian Government is somewhere around $90 billion. Canadian farmers quite rightly ask why similar amounts of money are not available to agriculture through the Farm Credit Corporation. They do not want that much money, but they would like some to be available to them. Why are farmers not given concessionary financing terms, such as those available to offshore customers through the Export Development Corporation? One Okanagan orchardist was forced to take out a loan with the FCC when interest rates were at their highest. He informs me that the has an extra $500 per month burden in interest charges over what he would pay at current rates. Also he told me that the only alternative available to him would be to borrow from a private lender, pay off the FCC and reapply to FCC for a new loan, because private lenders will not provide long-term credit. Of course, the hooker is that the FCC cannot give any assurance that money will be available. If the Government of Canada considers that Canadian exports require the financial commitments contained in Bill C-110, surely it is not too much to>uggest that agriculture, the largest job creator in the nation, is deserving of equal treatment.
I mentioned job creation because the obvious objective for providing this amount of money to the EDC is that it may end up in the creation of jobs in Canada in the manufacturing and in other sectors of the economy. We must remember that at the time when we favour one side of the economy we are neglecting agriculture. In the City of Penticton in my constituency, the Canadian Canners operation closed down last year, putting 300 people out of work. We have to look for a more balanced approach to the type of aid we provide industry, farmers or whatever.
Export Development Act
Bill C-110 totally discriminates and overlooks the need of the Government of Canada to appear interested in all areas of the economy and the need for the Government of Canada to accept accountability across the spectrum of economic activity in the nation.

Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members of my Party continue to rise to express their opposition to Bill C-110, surely it must be clearly evident to Hon. Members on the other side of the House that this is no ordinary piece of legislation. How many times must we on this side of the House rise before Government Members recognize that this is a serious issue? The wealth of Canadian taxpayers is not unlimited. The people of Canada expect and deserve accountability for the expenditure of their tax dollars. Unfortunately it is only Opposition Members and the Auditor General of Canada who show genuine concern for the public purse.
The amendments currently under discussion would go a long way toward making the Export Development Corporation and the Government more responsible. In a portion of the Bill under discussion today, the Government wishes to increase from $3.5 billion to $10 billion the amount of money which Cabinet may have at its disposal to insure export loans which the board of directors of the EDC has decided are too risky.
The Government will be entering into a series of high risk propositions to the tune of billions of dollars in order to support the export sector of the economy. We in this Party are arguing that $3.5 billion, half of which is presently unused, is more than enough to insure a series of what could easily be unsound export deals. Why should we put an additional $6.5 billion at risk? Perhaps the Government is pushing this particular portion of the legislation because it feels there may be some revenue to be generated by competing with insurance companies around the world. Nothing could be further from the truth. Mr. Culham, senior vice-president of finance of the EDC, told the standing committee dealing with Bill C-110 that EDC's $1.1 million profit reported last year was insignificant in relation to the billions of dollars of loan and insurance business the corporation handles each year. The Export Development Corporation should get out of the insurance business. There are private sector interests that could more adequately provide this service.
Unfortunately, the Government continues to believe in the infallibility of the public sector. It has almost no faith in the expertise which is readily available in the private sector. I mention this because it was made absolutely clear during the committee hearings. The Minister responsible for EDC was only vaguely aware of a paper presented to the corporation by the Royal Bank of Canada concerning the financing of Canadian exports. Why did the Minister not seriously consider the proposal of the country's largest bank, an organization which is well represented throughout the world? In the paper it compared the various methods of raising capital on the Euro-bond market, and concluded that it had been able to raise money at a lower cost than had the EDC. Surely this finding should interest the Minister. The Royal Bank plan

September 23, 1983
Export Development Act
called for not only increasing the involvement of our Canadian chartered banks in export financing, but also for the involvement of the 50-odd new foreign banks now operating in Canada.
The Bank Act passed in 1980 allows foreign banks to operate in Canada. These banks represent a host of nations from around the world. Why are they being excluded from helping to finance Canadian trade? Obviously this left leaning Government has a dislike for private sector organizations. Had the Royal Bank's proposal been accepted, it would have ensured that Canadians would become more effective exporters. It would have lessened the risk to Canadian taxpayers, to the extent that the Government would have had to borrow less through the EDC. Unfortunately, these proposals did not receive the attention they warranted and were countered by a 50-page paper from the EDC.
A further problem with this section of the Act is that it will only increase the Government's capacity to service these speculative types of ventures and will ultimately result in an unmandated form of foreign aid. We have foreign aid agencies with a mandate to do precisely that. The role of the EDC is to promote Canadian exports and, by so doing, to improve the Canadian economy. Its mandate should not be to serve as a foreign aid agency. By increasing its capacity to insure poor risks behind the backs of Parliamentarians, we are only increasing the likelihood that hundreds of millions of dollars will be squandered. What guarantees does the House have that insuring high risk export deals will in the end result in permanent jobs for Canadians? There are no guarantees whatsoever to taxpayers in the Bill. What is guaranteed is that the EDC will be unaccountable.
Motion No. 8 is simply a further attempt responsibly to control the Export Development Corporation. In the same manner that the previous motion would limit the amount Cabinet has at its disposal for insuring risky export ventures, this motion is designed to keep a realistic ceiling on the amount the directors of the corporation can use for loan guarantees. To increase the amount of financing available through the Consolidated Revenue Fund from $2.5 billion to $10 billion will have a twofold effect. First, it will of course lead to greater expenditures. Second, it will increase, not diminish, the problem of accountability. While this motion cannot solve the latter problem, it would succeed at least in going some distance toward correcting the former. If the Government has only $2.5 billion in the Consolidated Revenue Fund to use for loan guarantees, perhaps the Export Development Corporation will develop sharper business practices.
Last May, Mr. David Slater, Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, appeared before the standing committee to comment on Bill C-110. Mr. Slater offered these words of caution:
It should be noted that export subsidies are far from being the potent instruments governments seem to think they are in achieving their various macro-economic objectives.
As well, Mr. Slater said that it is a myth that loan subsidies from the Export Development Corporation are mostly aimed at giving exports that initial push, or assisting small or medium-size companies. The fact is, he said, large corporations receive most of the resources devoted to export assistance.
Finally, on the subject of private sector participation in the field of export finance, Mr. Slater said that the Export Development Corporation should encourage a greater direct involvement of private sector institutions. This was the advice of the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, not the chairman of the Royal Bank. Unfortunately, his words appear to have fallen on deaf ears.
In closing, allow me to make one further point. Canada has lost many opportunities to export goods in the international market. Bureaucracies are notorious for inaction. Contracts have been lost because the Export Development Corporation has been slow to act. In many instances, Canada has lost out because of keen foreign private sector competitors. What is wrong with sharing the financing of exporting Canadian goods with the private sector? It has the experience, the knowledge and the investment capital that is so necessary in this field. Why not spread the risks around?
We live in a pluralistic society, but it is becoming increasingly clear that our society is dominated by big government. The record of the Government in the field of export has deteriorated consistently over the past decade. It is time for a new approach, an approach that would utilize all sectors in our society, rather then excluding them from participating.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for the third time in this debate, and I count it a privilege to do just that. I note with interest the empty benches on the other side. Of the six or seven Liberals who are here, one is the Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) who has already told us that he is not going to participate in this debate. It seems a little ironic that one of the Ministers accountable to the people of Canada for external relations is not going to take part in a debate dealing with the Export Development Corporation. One would think that was part of the interest, if not the responsibility, that he should have in our foreign relations.
As we have debated Bill C-110, Mr. Speaker, we have talked about the growing number of Crown corporations and the growing freedom they enjoy in borrowing money, expending our indebtedness, and in making Canadians go further and further into debt from the day they are born. Motions Nos. 3 and 5 dealt specifically with the global borrowing capacity of the corporation. Now, on Motions Nos. 6 and 8 we are dealing with one aspect where the Cabinet, on its own initiative, by way of EDC can extend loan guarantees from the present $3.5 billion to $10 billion. It can lend outside of the parameters of EDC from $2.5 billion to $10 billion.
There has been a principle enunciated over and over again, Mr. Speaker, by Members on this side that the Parliament of Canada must assert its authority regarding the spending of the Government. When the Government has open-ended borrow-
September 23, 1983

ing authority, as it appears to have in this Bill, then the Parliament of Canada must assert itself. That is one of the fundamental principles of parliamentary democracy, the power of the purse. As we were debating that several days ago, 1 remember that one of my colleagues spoke of that very principle. We as Parliamentarians must have scrutiny over the spending power of the Government. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) sat there and said, "Well, that is what we are doing now." I remember his saying that, and I think he will freely admit that. It is not a big confession to make; he can handle that much. That highlighted the difference in the mindset of the Conservative Party from that of the Liberal Government. The Liberal approach has always been, "Give us global authority, we can do what we want, and that mandate is for anything we want to do." Nothing illustrates that more clearly, Mr. Speaker, than the election campaign in 1980 where the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went across Canada very quietly, which was uncharacteristic of him. It was almost impossible to get him to say anything. Then he got his mandate, and now he wants to be able to do anything. He did not debate the Constitution, the National Energy Program or any of those things during the election campaign, but now that he is elected, he thinks he can do anything. That is the principle the Government invokes in this kind of debate and in this kind of Bill: "Give us a mandate over $62 billion and then let us do as we wish."
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that there ought to be some strictures placed on this kind of open-ended spending. That is the principle of parliamentary authority. When you give the Cabinet the kind of mandate the clause in this Bill will do, it invariably goes sour because there is not enough of a check. It may be that we have very short memories as Canadians, but 1 think all of us still remember the kind of investment made in Jamaica on behalf of former Prime Minister Manley. It was for no other reason than to influence the elections of that particular Commonwealth country on behalf of Mr. Manley, because he happened to be a good friend of our Prime Minister and he happened to be of the same kind of political stripe as our Prime Minister. He was able to use the kind of authority this Bill gives to Cabinet to do the many things he did in Jamaica. When they can do that, it invariably is wrong. It is wrong in principle, Mr. Speaker, because it creates the wrong pattern. It shows differences of application between foreign companies and domestic ones.
I can understand the Government wanting to have as sweet a deal as it can to encourage foreign trade. All of us want to facilitate and encourage foreign trade. But when you treat foreign countries better than you treat your own citizens, there is something wrong. As we have noted before, and as my colleague mentioned earlier, there was this deal to build a monument in Algeria. I thought the deal was for 9.9 per cent, but my colleague tells me that the deal to construct the monument was for 7.5 per cent. If we can lend money for that kind of a deal when our people are paying 18 per cent to 24 per cent, then there is something wrong.
Export Development Act
1 have a company in my riding called Geramatic. It happens to be one of the best companies, not only in Canada but in the world, leaders in the field of hydraulic winches. Here is a company dealing in export, but in the last three months it has given notice that it has to move out of the country because it cannot function here any longer because of the cost of operation. That is the double standard of treatment. Foreign companies get a "sweetheart" deal in interest rates, but domestic companies have to pay the going rate of interest and, because of the cost of operation, have to move away. In this particular case, it affects 110 families in one fell swoop. This has occurred partly because of the National Energy Program, 1 might add. These companies are driven out of Canada.
if the Government is interested in our proposal, I would certainly invite it to make an arrangement whereby the principles that we have been addressing will be spoken to in the amendments that it brings forward. I would invite it to do so.

May I speak to the amendment for a moment, Mr. Speaker?
I would like to say to the House that this Party has, to this point, put up 140 speakers on report stage of the amendments that were before the House. We did that not because we in any way wanted to upset international trade. Indeed, we think it is essential that the trade of the country be promoted with the best efforts of all. However, it is most important for this Party and for the country that the people of the country know that the Parliament of Canada controls the spending of the Government of Canada and that agencies that are responsible to the Government of Canada are controlled by the Parliament of Canada.
This amendment will control the borrowing of the corporation to the actual capital and surplus of the corporation. In that sense, the corporation will not be able to run away with itself. It will be under the strict control of Parliament, and we think that this amendment is exceptionally important and is the kind of thing we as a Party stand for.
Hear, hear!
